entries.clue: Between adults, terrible crime Trump controls it (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The country is named by the man who runs it rather than by a synonym, so a whole clause stands where a proper noun would.

indicatorNotes.Between: What lies between two things has them standing either side of it, so the shuffled letters are written inside the pair.
indicatorNotes.terrible: Something terrible has gone badly wrong, and letters in a bad way do not keep the order they were printed in.

blocks.note: A was the British cinema certificate for an adult audience, and two adults make two of them, one for each side
five letters to be re-set between the pair

annotation.surface: A dreadful offence committed between consenting grown-ups, in a country with a known owner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trump controls it' looks like the setter's sour aside at the end of a sentence about crime, and it is the definition — the only part naming the entry. Adults come in a pair because the certificate is a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Donald Trump is the president of the United States, so the country is the 'it' he controls, named by its owner rather than described.

entries.clue: Forces liar dithering with it into well! (8)

indicatorNotes.dithering: Somebody dithering cannot settle on anything, so the letters beside the word will not settle into the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.into: What goes into a thing ends up inside it, so those letters are written between the two the exclamation supplies.

blocks.note: 'My!' is the exclamation of surprise that 'well!' also is; it parts to take what goes inside
four letters to be re-set
two more letters joining the shuffle

annotation.surface: A wavering fibber being dropped down a well.
annotation.walkthrough: Well is the exclamation, not the hole in the ground, and the clue's own exclamation mark is the only sign of it. Forces sits at the head looking like a verb and is the plural noun for a country's armed services.
annotation.definitionFit: A country's military is its army, navy and air force taken together, which is what the forces names in British usage.

entries.clue: Our Mr Blair getting elevated – prepare for a quick getaway! (3,2)

blocks.note: Private Eye has run its St Albion Parish News for years with Tony Blair writing as the parish vicar, so the magazine's own Mr Blair holds a clergyman's title
something elevated has been raised, and raised is up

annotation.surface: A former prime minister moving up in the world, with a fast exit to get ready for.
annotation.walkthrough: The Eye has cast Tony Blair as a vicar since his first term, writing the St Albion parish newsletter, which is what makes 'Our Mr Blair' a title rather than a name. The dash does the joining and instructs nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: To rev up an engine is to race it while the car is still standing, which is exactly what a driver does before pulling away fast.

entries.clue: Actor, on 'performing' strip perhaps (7)

indicatorNotes.performing: Something performing is going through its paces rather than standing still, so the letters in front are set down in another arrangement.

blocks.note: seven letters to be re-set, the comma no obstacle

annotation.surface: An actor taking his turn in a striptease.
annotation.walkthrough: Strip is the tease on the surface and the row of drawn panels a newspaper prints underneath, with 'perhaps' admitting it is one kind of strip among several. The quotation marks round performing are the setter pointing at the word twice.
annotation.definitionFit: A cartoon is the drawing that fills a comic strip, so strip names the answer by the form it is usually printed in.

entries.clue: Gangsters lie around somewhere in Alabama (6)

indicatorNotes.around: Something moved around has been shifted out of where it was, so the three letters beside the word are set down in another order.

blocks.note: the mob is the collective name for organised criminals
the three letters of the word, re-set

annotation.surface: Mobsters loafing about in the Deep South.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lie around' is one idle phrase on the surface and splits cleanly: the first word is the letters, the second the instruction. The state is given because the word on its own would read as the telephone in your pocket.
annotation.definitionFit: Mobile is the port city on Alabama's Gulf coast, the state's only seaport, so the state is enough to place it.

entries.clue: Kiss and fondle but be perceptive? (4,3)

blocks.note: American slang for a long session of kissing and groping in the back of a car
the sense used of a shape in fog or a signature on a cheque: to succeed in seeing what is there

annotation.surface: Advice to a lover: get your hands busy but keep your wits about you.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark is honest about the second half, which asks for the ability rather than the act — discerning something faint at the edge of sight. 'But' is doing nothing beyond making the two senses sound like one piece of advice.
annotation.definitionFit: Kissing and fondling is the American slang sense, and the other is discerning something faint — the fog-bound shape you finally see.

entries.clue: No support for ministerial arses (9)

blocks.note: reads as nobody backing the ministers, and means the seats that are not theirs — in the Commons the government's ministers fill the front row and everyone else sits behind them
the Eye's word for the members who park themselves there, and a bench is the one piece of Commons furniture built for a row of them

annotation.surface: Nobody willing to prop up the ministers' backsides.
annotation.walkthrough: Support is the word doing double duty: backing a minister on the surface, and the thing a bench either has or does not have. Nothing in the six words hands over a letter, so they have to be read twice instead.
annotation.definitionFit: The back benches are the Commons rows behind the front bench, seating exactly those MPs who hold no ministerial office.

entries.clue: Toxic, all the crap (6)

indicatorNotes.crap: Crap is British for rubbish, and letters called rubbish are not to be trusted to stay in the order they were printed.

blocks.note: six letters to be re-set

annotation.surface: A blunt verdict that the whole lot of it is worthless.
annotation.walkthrough: 'All the crap' reads as one dismissive phrase and works as two: the first two words are the letters, the third is the instruction to shake them. Toxic is the definition and does its job in a single word at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A lethal dose is one that kills, and toxic is the adjective for the substance that does it — the two share the language of warning labels.

entries.clue: (& 15dn/22dn.) IT bumf I circulated with far right, like a good boss? (4)

indicatorNotes.circulated: To circulate is to go round and round the office, so the letters named come back to rest in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: bumf is British office slang for paperwork nobody reads; seven letters here, the I taken as the letter it is
three more letters joining the shuffle
R is the standard short form for right

annotation.surface: Computer paperwork going round the office, pushed by someone at the far right of politics.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Far right' splits in two: the first word goes into the mixture whole and the second contributes only its initial. Eleven letters spread over three entries is why the count feels wrong until the cross-references are read.
annotation.definitionFit: Firm but fair is the stock British verdict on a boss who holds the line without playing favourites, which is what makes one good to work for.

entries.clue: Smart arse about to get lifting device put on penis (6,4)

blocks.note: c is the short form of circa, the Latin for about
a lever is the bar you bear down on to raise a weight
the commonest playground word for it

annotation.surface: A know-all about to have a hoist fitted to his genitals.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as the idiom 'about to' and is the crossword's single letter for circa, which leaves 'to get' with nothing to do but join. Smart arse is the definition, printed in full because this is the Eye.
annotation.definitionFit: A clever dick is someone who parades how much he knows, which is the person British English calls a smart arse.

entries.clue: Nick, ultimately the most appealing (4)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Most' marks the degree rather than a grammatical superlative: the answer is the plain adjective for appealing, and the clue pushes it to the top of that scale.

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end, so only the last letter of the word beside it is taken.

blocks.note: to nick yourself shaving is to cut yourself
the last letter of the word, taken on its own

annotation.surface: Somebody called Nick turning out to be the pick of the bunch.
annotation.walkthrough: Nick reads as a man's name and works as the small cut you give yourself shaving. The definite article is the least noticeable word in the sentence and the one carrying a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Cute is what we call something appealing in a small, endearing way — a kitten, a baby's shoe — so appealing is the sense and 'most' the setter's emphasis.

entries.clue: On and off second attempt to grab chest (4-2)

indicatorNotes.to grab: To grab a thing is to take hold of it, so the letters named next are held between the two pieces already in hand.

blocks.note: s is the clock's short form for second
a top is the garment worn over the chest
a go at something is an attempt at it

annotation.surface: A second, on-and-off attempt at a grope.
annotation.walkthrough: Chest is a garment word here, not the ribcage or the furniture, and the two pieces that close round it are not even adjacent in the clue. 'On and off' is the definition and names the halting way an economy is run.
annotation.definitionFit: Stop-go describes anything that keeps halting and restarting — traffic, or an economic policy of alternating brake and accelerator — which is what happening on and off means.

entries.clue: Flash Ray's night light (8)

blocks.note: to moon is to bare your backside at somebody, which is one way of flashing
a beam of light is a ray of it

annotation.surface: A character called Flash Ray and the lamp he keeps by the bed.
annotation.walkthrough: Flash Ray reads as one man's nickname, which is what hides the seam between the two halves. Mooning is the British word for dropping your trousers at somebody, and that is the sense wanted, not speed.
annotation.definitionFit: A moonbeam is the shaft of moonlight that comes through a window after dark, which is light by night in the plainest sense.

entries.clue: Doughty type has jar (not pissed) (6)

indicatorNotes.pissed: Pissed is British for drunk, and a drunk keeps nothing in the order it should be, so the letters beside the word are re-set.

blocks.note: three letters to be re-set
three more letters joining the shuffle, the bracket no obstacle

annotation.surface: A hardy sort with a drink in his hand, insisting he is sober.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not pissed' is a claim of sobriety on the surface and splits down the middle underneath: the first word joins the letters, the second shakes them. Working like a Trojan is the idiom the definition leans on, and it is about effort, not ancient Troy.
annotation.definitionFit: To work like a Trojan is to work doggedly and without complaint, so a Trojan is a doughty type — stout-hearted and not to be worn down.

entries.clue: "Try getting males transported at first" –  which comes from the Supreme Court? (9)

annotation.definition: which comes from the Supreme Court
annotation.definitionNote: The entry is named by where it comes from rather than by a synonym, so a relative clause stands where a noun would.

indicatorNotes.at first: At first means at the beginning, so only the opening letter of the word in front of it is taken.

blocks.note: to try a case is to judge it, which is what a court is for
males of the species, in the plural
the first letter of the word, taken on its own

annotation.surface: A line quoted from the bench: have the men shipped off to the colonies.
annotation.walkthrough: Transportation was the sentence that shipped British convicts to Australia, which is why the quoted words sound like a judge speaking — and that whole word yields one letter. 'Try' is the courtroom verb, not the attempt the sentence wants.
annotation.definitionFit: A judgement is the ruling a court hands down, and the Supreme Court is the highest court in the United Kingdom, so the clue names the thing by its source.

entries.clue: Fail to make a declaration, getting some stick? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The two halves read the same letters differently: one is a noun, the other a cricketing verb phrase of two words that the grid runs together.

blocks.note: the short rod a relay runner hands on, or the one a conductor waves at an orchestra
in cricket a captain may declare to end his side's innings early, and one who does not simply leaves his batsmen at the crease

annotation.surface: A captain refusing to declare and taking criticism for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Getting some stick' is British for being on the receiving end of criticism, which is what the surface means and not what the definition wants. Decline to declare and your side bats on — two words the grid runs together as one.
annotation.definitionFit: A baton is a stick, the relay runner's or the conductor's, and batting on is what a side does when its captain declines to declare.

entries.clue: see 8dn.
It would probably not be hard being this powerless (8)

annotation.definition2: It would probably not be hard being this
annotation.definitionNote: The second half names the condition by what it means for 'it' rather than by a synonym, so a whole clause stands where an adjective would.

blocks.clueFragment: It would probably not be hard being this
blocks.note: 'it' is the Eye's word for the male member, and hard is the state it fails to reach
the straight sense: having no power to act or to change anything

annotation.surface: A gloomy forecast of what will not be happening tonight.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves define, which is why no part of the sentence hands over a letter. The plain word is used of governments and protesters as readily as of men, and the clue counts on you hearing only the man.
annotation.definitionFit: Powerless is the plain sense, unable to act or effect anything, and the other half is the specifically sexual one, a man unable to get an erection.

entries.clue: Got drunk to back Arsenal? (5)

indicatorNotes.back: To go back is to go the other way, and along an across entry that is right to left, so the word named is written in reverse.

blocks.note: to tope is to drink steadily, so a man who got drunk toped; those five letters are then read the other way

annotation.surface: Getting drunk in support of a football club.
annotation.walkthrough: Arsenal is the north London football club on the surface and a store of weapons underneath, which is the older meaning and the one the question mark flags. Tope is a verb the Victorians used and crosswords have kept alive.
annotation.definitionFit: A depot is a military store where arms and supplies are held, which is what an arsenal is before the word became a football club.

entries.clue: Scoff "In jail!" (3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The quoted half names where the man ends up rather than what is done to him, so a prepositional phrase stands where a verb phrase would.

blocks.note: British slang for eating fast and greedily — scoffing the lot before anyone else gets a look in
the sentence a judge passes, and where the convicted man goes to serve it

annotation.surface: A jeer flung at somebody: that is where you are going.
annotation.walkthrough: Scoff is doing two jobs before the wordplay even starts — the jeer the quotation marks suggest, and the British verb for eating greedily, which is the sense wanted. Three words of clue leave nowhere for an indicator to hide.
annotation.definitionFit: To put away a plate of food is to eat the lot, and to put a man away is to send him to prison: one phrasal verb, two settled senses.

entries.clue: Connive to be seen in Porsche, Mercedes ... (6)

indicatorNotes.to be seen in: What can be seen in something is sitting there already, so the letters are taken unchanged from inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters run on across the comma and the word break, in the order written

annotation.surface: Angling to be spotted in expensive German cars.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma between the two marques sits exactly where the letters cross, and punctuation is no barrier to a concealed word. The ellipsis leads the eye on to the next clue and carries no instruction at all.
annotation.definitionFit: To scheme is to lay plans with your own advantage in mind, which is what connive means when it is not about turning a blind eye.

entries.clue: The chief perversion of Euro MPs (7)

indicatorNotes.perversion of: A perversion is a twisting of something out of its proper shape, so the letters that follow come out in another order.

blocks.note: seven letters to be re-set

annotation.surface: European parliamentarians and the vice the papers accuse them of.
annotation.walkthrough: Perversion carries the Eye's usual insinuation on the surface and is a plain shuffle instruction underneath. MPs sit at Westminster, so the Euro in front of them is the setter borrowing a parliament, not an abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: A supremo is the person in sole charge of an operation, the one everybody else answers to, which is what calling somebody the chief means.

entries.clue: Agitate for prison in rebellion (4,2)

blocks.note: stir is old British slang for prison — a convict does his time in stir
a crowd or a country in rebellion has risen, and is said to be up

annotation.surface: Campaigning for a jail sentence in the middle of an uprising.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'up' looks like an instruction to read letters from the bottom of the column, and here it is simply two of them. Stir for prison goes back to Victorian slang and is still what British crime writers reach for.
annotation.definitionFit: To stir up trouble is to work it into being, and agitate is the same verb one register higher — both are what a rabble-rouser does to a crowd.

entries.clue: (& 24dn.) Press revelations: "The Eye's reprehensible way!" (6,2)

blocks.note: what the column prints: the stories newspapers and their owners would rather not see printed about themselves
'way' and 'reprehensible' are the two ordinary words the name is built out of, and the magazine you are holding has run the column under it since the 1970s

annotation.surface: The magazine denouncing the disgraceful conduct of the newspapers.
annotation.walkthrough: Fleet Street was the home of the national press for a century, and Private Eye's name for it has outlived the papers' move east. Nothing in the sentence yields letters: the quoted half is the title read as if it were a phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Street of Shame is Private Eye's own long-running column of stories about what newspapers and their proprietors get up to, so press revelations is exactly its contents.

entries.clue: see 8dn.
Firearm carried by Trump is tolerated (6)

indicatorNotes.carried by: What is carried by something is borne along inside it, so the letters sit unbroken within the words that follow.

blocks.note: the letters run on from inside the name and straight across the two words after it

annotation.surface: A gun the president is allowed to carry about with him.
annotation.walkthrough: The span begins inside the president's name, which is the last place a solver looks because capital letters read as a thing rather than as letters. 'Carried by' is the concealment instruction and sounds like a man with a weapon on him.
annotation.definitionFit: A pistol is the handgun small enough to carry in a pocket or a holster, the plainest example of a firearm there is.

entries.clue: see 21ac.
A Republican almost determined to be garrulous politician's source? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is named by the idiom it belongs to rather than by a synonym: a politician talking rubbish is said to be talking out of it, so a possessive phrase stands where a noun would.

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost means not quite all the way, so the word it touches stops one letter short of its end.

blocks.note: the article, taken as it stands
R is the letter printed beside a Republican's name on an American ballot
somebody determined on a course is set on it, and the word gives up its last letter

annotation.surface: An American Republican who has nearly made his mind up and will not stop talking.
annotation.walkthrough: Talking out of one's arse is the British idiom for talking rubbish, which is what the definition points at and why the question mark is there. Three separate pieces inside four letters is as tight as a charade gets.
annotation.definitionFit: A politician who talks endless rubbish is said to be talking out of his arse, and the idiom makes that the place his words come from.

entries.clue: Bill's predecessor getting pale daily? (5,5)

blocks.note: a pale face has the colour drained out of it
a daily is a newspaper that comes out every weekday

annotation.surface: The man who had the job before Bill, turning paler by the day.
annotation.walkthrough: A British government sets out its intentions in a white paper first and publishes the bill afterwards, so the capital B is the whole misdirection — it reads as a man's name. The question mark admits daily is one kind of paper among many.
annotation.definitionFit: A white paper is the policy document a British government publishes before drafting the bill it becomes, so it comes first in the same process.

entries.clue: Indifference of 'one-touch', heartless Home Secretary (6)

indicatorNotes.heartless: Something heartless has had its middle taken out, so only the outermost letters of what follows survive.

blocks.note: one of a thing is a, the indefinite article
a pat on the back is a light touch of the hand
the first letter of the first word and the last of the second, with everything between them gone

annotation.surface: A cold-hearted minister accused of governing with one touch and caring about none of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One-touch' is in quotation marks because it is two separate pieces of wordplay rather than the football phrase. The Home Secretary is the cabinet minister responsible for policing and immigration in Britain, and it is the office title that is wanted, not whoever holds it.
annotation.definitionFit: Apathy is the state of not caring enough to act, which is what indifference names — both nouns for the same absence of feeling.

entries.clue: Reserve fashion house for porky types (7)

blocks.note: the mode is what is in fashion, the word borrowed straight from the French
a sty is the pen a pig is kept in

annotation.surface: Booking a designer label for customers on the large side.
annotation.walkthrough: Reserve is the noun, the quality of not pushing yourself forward, and reads as the verb 'book' at the head of the sentence. Porky is British for fat, so the house being asked for is a pig's.
annotation.definitionFit: Modesty is the reserve of somebody who plays down their own abilities, and reserve is that same restraint named as a quality.
